title: The Ethiopian Eunuch: Inclusion in the Kingdom
paragraphs: The Ethiopian Eunuch: Inclusion in the Kingdom

He had power.
He had position.
He had access to wealth, influence, government, and prestige.
But he was still riding home empty.
That is the tragedy nobody sees.

You can sit close to power and still feel far from God.
You can travel to worship and still not know Him.
You can read holy words and still not understand the way of salvation.
That was the Ethiopian eunuch.

A man of authority.
A man of responsibility.
A man returning from Jerusalem.
A man reading Isaiah in his chariot.
And still... searching.
Acts 8:27–28 says:

“And behold, a man of Ethiopia, an eunuch of great authority under Candace queen of the Ethiopians, who had the charge of all her treasure, and had come to Jerusalem for to worship,
Was returning, and sitting in his chariot read Esaias the prophet.”
Read that again.

He had come to worship.
But worship attendance is not the same as new birth.
Religious activity is not the same as reconciliation with God.
That is where many people are right now.

You know the language.
You know the culture.
You know the songs.
You know when to bow your head and when to say “amen.”
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
You can be near sacred things and still be outside peace with God.

The eunuch carried a deeper tension than politics or status. In the ancient world, he would have known exclusion. He would have known what it meant to stand near, but not fully inside. He would have known the ache of distance. He had a scroll in his hands, but unanswered questions in his soul.
And God saw it.

Not just the chariot.
Not just the road.
Not just the scroll.
God saw the man.

This is the glory of the Gospel: God does not only summon the clean, the qualified, the insiders, the socially accepted, the ceremonially welcomed. He seeks the outsider. He pursues the one who has been marked, wounded, disqualified in the eyes of men.

Because the Kingdom of God is not built on human gatekeeping.
It is opened by Jesus Christ.
Acts 8:29–31 says:

“Then the Spirit said unto Philip, Go near, and join thyself to this chariot.
And Philip ran thither to him, and heard him read the prophet Esaias, and said, Understandest thou what thou readest?
And he said, How can I, except some man should guide me?...”
That line is heavy.
“How can I...?”
He was reading truth without seeing the Person the truth was pointing to.

That is spiritual blindness.
And no amount of education, morality, or effort can heal it.

You do not need more self-improvement.
You need revelation.
You need Christ.
The eunuch was reading from Isaiah 53, the chapter soaked in blood, sorrow, substitution, and salvation.
Acts 8:32–33 says:

“He was led as a sheep to the slaughter; and like a lamb dumb before his shearer, so opened he not his mouth:
In his humiliation his judgment was taken away: and who shall declare his generation? for his life is taken from the earth.”

He was reading about suffering.
He was reading about rejection.
He was reading about a man crushed, humiliated, cut off.
And maybe that is why this mattered so deeply.

Because the broken can recognize brokenness.
The rejected can feel the weight of rejection.
The cut-off know what it means to be cut off.

But Isaiah 53 is not merely about pain.
It is about substitution.
Isaiah 53:5–6 says:

“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.”
There it is.

Not inspiration.
Not moral advice.
Not “do better.”

Sin.
Judgment.
A Substitute.
Grace.

Philip did not give him a motivational speech.
Philip did not tell him to believe in himself.
Philip did not tell him that all spiritual paths lead to God.
No.
Acts 8:35 says:
“Then Philip opened his mouth, and began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus.”
Jesus.

Not religion without blood.
Not ethics without atonement.
Not spirituality without repentance.
Jesus Christ.

This is the center of everything.
The eunuch was not saved by being sincere.
He was not saved by making a pilgrimage.
He was not saved by handling a scroll.
He was not saved by his status, his humility, or his curiosity.
He was confronted with Jesus.

The Son of God.
The Lamb of God.
The crucified Messiah.
The risen Lord.
The only name by which sinners are saved.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:

“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
And this is where inclusion in the Kingdom becomes shocking.

Because the question is not: Are you impressive enough?
The question is not: Are you clean enough?
The question is not: Do people approve of you?
The question is: What have you done with Jesus Christ?

The Kingdom does not open because you finally become worthy.
The Kingdom opens because Christ was worthy in your place.
God had spoken of this long before.
Isaiah 56:3–5 says:

A place.
A name.
Within My walls.
Do you see it?

What law exposed, grace in Christ redeems.
What distance revealed, Jesus removes.
What exclusion symbolized, the Gospel overturns.

Not by pretending sin is small.
Not by erasing holiness.
But by satisfying justice at the cross.

That is the difference between human inclusion and Gospel inclusion.
The world includes by lowering standards.
God includes by fulfilling righteousness in His Son.
Read that again.

The cross is not God ignoring sin.
The cross is God punishing sin in Christ so sinners who repent and believe can be brought near.
Romans 3:23–24 says:

“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God;
Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.”
All have sinned.

That includes the visibly broken and the publicly respected.
The religious and the rebellious.
The outsider and the insider.

You.
Me.
All.

God saw it.
You knew.

That hidden pride.
That secret lust.
That bitterness you keep feeding.
That image management.
That performance Christianity.
That private rebellion dressed in public respectability.
Spiritual diagnosis: your greatest problem is not exclusion by people, but separation from God because of sin.

And your greatest need is not affirmation.
It is redemption.

So when the eunuch heard Jesus preached, something happened.
Hope came alive.
Acts 8:36 says:
“And as they went on their way, they came unto a certain water: and the eunuch said, See, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized?”
Listen to that cry.
What hinders me?

That is the cry of every soul that has lived under the shadow of distance.
Every person who thinks, Surely not me.
Every person who believes grace is for cleaner people, better people, less stained people.
What hinders me?
Philip’s answer strikes at the center.
Acts 8:37 says:
“And Philip said, If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest. And he answered and said, I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.”
There it is.

Not pedigree.
Not ceremony first.
Not works.
Faith in Jesus Christ.
That is the doorway into the Kingdom.

And yes, true faith produces obedience.
Yes, baptism matters.
Yes, repentance is real.
But the ground of salvation is Christ alone, received by faith.
The eunuch went down into the water not to earn entrance, but because he had found the King.
And when he came up, he did not leave with a theory.
He left with joy.
Acts 8:39 says:
“...he went on his way rejoicing.”
Rejoicing.

Because when Jesus saves a man, He does not merely adjust behavior.
He gives peace.
He gives adoption.
He gives belonging.
He gives a new name, a new future, a new heart.
This is inclusion in the Kingdom.

Not token acceptance.
Not sentimental tolerance.
Not emotional comfort without truth.
This is a blood-bought welcome for repentant sinners through Jesus Christ.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
And maybe this is your story too.

You know what it feels like to stand on the edge.
To carry shame.
To carry questions.
To carry the silent belief that everyone else gets in, but not you.
But here is the truth:
John 6:37
“...him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
In no wise.

Not because your past is light.
Not because your record is clean.
Not because your wounds are imaginary.
But because Jesus Christ is mighty to save.

So repent.
Turn from sin.
Stop hiding behind religion, excuses, intellect, pain, or delay.
Come to Christ.

The road to Gaza was deserted.
But Heaven was not absent there.
And the same God who sent Philip to a searching man still sends His Word today.

To the broken.
To the ashamed.
To the outsider.
To the religious but empty.
To the one whispering, What hinders me?

Nothing hinders you—
except unbelief.

Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ.
Trust the One who was wounded for transgressors.
Trust the Lamb who was slaughtered for sinners.
Trust the risen King who brings the far-off near.
Ephesians 2:13 says:
“But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.”

Far off.
Made near.
By the blood of Christ.

That is the Gospel.
That is the Kingdom.
That is your invitation.

Decision moment:
Will you keep reading about Him from a distance?
Or will you bow to Him as Lord?
